## Editor's Brief

Markets navigated a contradictory 24 hours, with geopolitical whiplash—a U.S. strike on Iranian targets after a tanker hit in the Strait of Hormuz, followed by futures surging on a reported U.S.-Iran deal—competing against a hawkish Federal Reserve and a deepening tech rout. The S&P 500 slid below its 50-day moving average while the Nasdaq suffered its worst week in months as Wall Street rotated out of technology. Simultaneously, a memory-chip crunch is rattling Apple and Microsoft and proving existential for smaller hardware firms, while SpaceX’s fast-track inclusion into the Nasdaq-100 promises a wave of ETF buying. In Europe, the German auto industry announced historic job cuts as Chinese EV rivals flood the market, and Trump threatened 100% tariffs on European digital-service taxes. China’s auto sector faces its own headwinds: NIO’s CEO warned of a 20% sales plunge, even as Li Auto expanded into Macao. On the positive side, Citi called beaten-down Chinese internet stocks a buying opportunity, A-share IPO fundraising hit nearly 70 billion yuan, and Hong Kong leads global ultra-rich population growth. Retail sentiment in Chinese social-media communities turned cautiously optimistic, with record-breaking private-equity fund counts and a rebound in gold and crypto prices.

- **U.S.-Iran Flashpoint:** A commercial tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz, prompting U.S. military retaliation, yet futures quickly rallied on news of a potential deal. The dueling narratives have sent oil and crypto higher, but the 60-day ceasefire framework is now in doubt.
